blocks.x: Okay, let's get your name on here first.
You say you want to get my name? Mm-hmm. Well, you want me to spell it because I don't think you spell my name right.
Okay.
My name is Paul Barberin. P-A-U-L, Paul, B-A-R-B-A-R-I-N, Paul Barberin.
How do you spell it?
Some folks call me, you know, it's a Creole name, you know, French descent. How do you spell Adolph?
How do you spell Adolph?
Oh, you want the other name you want. Oh, the middle name, what I don't use. Oh, I see. A-D-O-L-P-H, Adolph. Yeah, that's my name.
And who were you named after?
Well, I was named after my dad because my dad is an Isidore. Isidore. No, that is Isidore. John Barberin.
Is that J-O-H-N or J-E-A-N, John? J-O-H-N.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah. I see.
Thanks for the coffee, Paul.
This is mine, I think. Let's see, I better put my name on here, Dick Allen.
Yeah, you would put Dick Allen.
Paul Crawford. Okay, and let's see, what's today's date on the mountain? December the... 23rd.
23rd, tomorrow is Christmas Eve. Okay, 1959. 1959, and we're at 818 St. Peter Street. Yeah, that's right.
All right. You wanted to tell me your exact address where you were born. Oh, my...
Well, I can't tell you the number, I can't recall the number of the house, but it's at the corner Barracks and St. Claude. On Barracks and St. Claude. Is it standing today?
The front of the house is facing Barracks Street.
Standing today? Sure. Is the house standing today? Well, yes, it is, but they're remodeled quite naturally, you know what I mean? After all that many years. Which corner is it?
Is it the lake or river corner? Oh, that's on the river.
Oh, the lake side of it.
On the lake side of Uptown? Yeah, Uptown River.
Uptown Lake Corner. Okay. You're going to give us a real year you were born this time or you're going to tell us? Well, I'm going to give you 1901. All right. I'm used to that. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. It seemed like later on they changed it, I don't know, but 1901 is what I am. That's May the 5th too.
Yeah, okay. Were there any musicians in the neighborhood where you grew up?
No, not so many, no, no, not so many at that time, no.
I thought you might remember hearing some.
No, no, no, I was quite, no, I was too small to remember. Too small to remember. I remember not yet.
Did you ever hear Buddy Bowman the first time?

Well, I tell you, I heard him, but I didn't see him and my mama told me we was living in the back of Police of Burns Hall. We lived on the airport street and Police of Burns Hall happened to be on Village Street and we lived in the back of Police of Burns Hall and every Monday used to have a lot of banquets. We called them banquets. People nowadays say banquets. I said banquets. Every Monday had a banquets at this particular hall, nearly every Monday. And especially Monday, well, my mama told me that Buddy Bowman was blowing. So that man's going to blow his brains out. Blows too loud. She said that Buddy Bowman, that's the only thing I knew about it.
You remember that, huh? No.
That's the only thing I could wrap.
She told you about it later or you remember it?
No, no, that day, that same day. You remember that. When he was blowing, yeah, that same day.
Well, how old were you then? What would you get?
Oh, let's see. I can't recall a day. I really can't.
You had a long banter, anything? No, no.
You were just tiny, huh? A tiny boy, a little boy. Mm-hmm.
I can't tell you about the earliest tunes you remember hearing, either in your home or played by bands.
Oh, the early tunes I heard. Mm-hmm. Well, most of all of them was Rags, I mean.
Mm-hmm. Remember any of the names of them?
Oh, yeah. African Pats, Ophelia Rag, Entertainers Rag, A Few Clothes. Oh, no.
A Few Clothes, I never heard that. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh, well, Grace and Beauty or Maple Leaf Rag, other rags, most of all of them.
You remember how Few Clothes went, anything about it?
No, I don't know. Mm-hmm. What's going to ask you about it? I wish I did because I never seen it. I never seen it written.
I never have seen Few Clothes in the Island of the Island. No, I haven't seen it. I've seen those others, you know, playing the Red Bull.
No, no, I've never seen that one. I wish I could remember because it's a good rag.
Yeah. Um, I was also wondering about your grandmother's picnics on the lake. You one time mentioned that, I'll tell you.

Yeah. Oh, I'm one of these have picnics out of lake, a bunch of training up. Mm-hmm. Out there. Mm-hmm. Have a good time all the time. Very good time. You want to smoke a mirror, you know, smoke a mirror. You heard about smoke a mirror. Yeah. You don't know, road smoke. And boy, when you got on smoke a mirror, you thought you were going to California someplace. Going five miles. Five mile ride. Smoke a mirror. Oh boy. Chaka chaka chaka chaka chaka chaka chaka chaka chaka chaka chaka. That's the way smoke a mirror went. It's just the way she went. How fast? Making about, well, she's making about, I see about seven miles an hour. Made more noise than anything. About seven miles an hour.
Where did your grandmother have those picnics?
Let's see if I can recall the name of that camp. Lucian Pavilion.
That was at?
Lucian Pavilion. That was at Millersburg? That's right.
Well, what was her deal? Did she run them herself? Yeah, she did them herself. Or just be for the family?

No, you see, that old lady, which is my father's mother, I mean, she'd feature entertainment, entertainment at that sort, you know? She liked to have parties and things like those, or picnics. And, well, she'd give a lot of parties at home for, you know, friends and things like that. I usually like to entertain, just entertain all the time.
Would you sell tickets to Lucian Pavilion, or was that just for friends?
I know that people would come, I mean, no tickets, you're just mouth to mouth, you know what I mean? Friends, you know what I mean?
There was no charge, in other words?
No, no, no charge, you'll bring your basket, you know, mouth to mouth and have a picnic. Well, that's a basket picnic, you know? Yeah.
When did she stop giving those picnics?

Oh, I was quite young, I can't recall that. They used to have a lot of bands out there, I can tell you that. They had bands on the sun in most every camp on that lake. All sorts of bands. Emile Krishmi could tell you that. He played a lot of those picnics.
Well, at that time, what days were the best, I'd have known about? On Sunday. Were there any other days for picnics?

Oh, well, well, yes, Monday was a good day, I mean, for those clubs, you know, like the Lions Club, and, you know, Bill's Club, pleasure clubs like that, you know, we get a picnic at the Aleutian Pavilion on Monday, she died.

While we're going through this, let's go through a typical week, you know what I mean? Like, in the life of a musician, what days, say, would be best for funerals? What days would be best for parades? What days would be best for bunkage? What days would be best for dance hall jobs? What days would be the best for going out of town?

Well, I'll tell you, let's go back to the dance hall, like the column in the hopes hall. Well, Monday night was always the best night. It was always the best night, Monday night. And then we had a good time. And then we had a good time. And a beer was a nickel, a glass of beer. So you take a dollar and change the dollar, twenty nickels, and you have your ball, I'm telling you. You buy your supper. Gumbo. I think gumbo at that time was fifteen cents a plate. Yeah, fifteen cents a plate. Yeah, fifteen cents a plate. Yeah, fifteen cents a plate. And then we had a beer, a nickel, a glass of beer. And then we had bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo Yeah, they were the best.
Well did they have white?
Most of the white, I mean, most of the white.
They had white and colored at Mellenberg at the same time.

Well yes, I mean, they didn't mix, I mean, you know. But one would run a camp next to the other. Yeah, right, yeah, like that, yeah. Everybody was very friendly and got along very nicely. All musicians, everybody in those days, I mean, that was swell, you know.
How much sitting in?

No, I didn't sit in there. I mean, the guys would be bucking one another, you know what I mean about it, blowing at each other, you know. And sometimes we'd have 10 bands, maybe 15 bands playing all at the same time. You ever use a code of music and you know what was happening? Well, the people that was dancing to the music wouldn't know, you know, right then and there, you know. Right on that spot, you know, particular spot. They wouldn't know unless we'd stop playing or somebody else would stop playing. And the band where you was at, you know, playing, maybe here's another band, playing far away, I wonder who was that one. All the bands was ratty, you know, they had some ratty bands. I mean, both bands, I mean, both races, I mean, the white and the inter-colored race, you know. They had good bands. They had good bands. I remember a band called, I just mentioned his dance, well, Emil Christian, man. The Christian band. Was that Emil Christian?
There were several of them, there's Charlie and Frank, too.
I don't know, I know it was Christian's band, that's all I know. Because they used to play at Lidgetfield and Royale, because the 5th Precinct was right next door.
And you visited there often?
No, I used to go around there, I mean, listen to them quicker. They used to play on the outside first, on the gallery, come out on the gallery and play. I wanted to run into the gallery, man.
I thought maybe you were in the 5th Precinct.

No, no, I don't see that 5th Precinct. Let me tell you about that 5th Precinct, or the first time with the 5th Precinct. It was either the first time, the second time. I went there twice. Off and up, you know. That's right, I played a job with Chris Kelly on a court, it was a house party on a court between Maraday and Manifel. And, well, the pay wasn't much, I think it was a dollar quarter, the pay was about a dollar quarter. It might have been a dollar. But the people was giving us quarters, a nickel, a dime, you know, Tim was to play, you know, this tune, play that tune. And when we got off, Chris Kelly was dividing the money at the corner of Wakewater and Maraday on a light there. And Chris happened to give somebody a quarter too much. He said, I'm shocked, because I had so much money. And nobody had it. So they started a big argument, you know. And I thought, I didn't have anything to do with that. You know, I didn't take the water off. So I started walking off. I put my drum, my bass drum on my back. You know, those days you had to carry a drum, strap on the back and get a snare drum in the sack. You know, you had that, but a pedal and a cymbal, you know. And I started walking off. I walked the hitter. So they almost came to blows, you know. So when we reached the corner of a, before we reached the corner of a, a Quarton Frenchman, the two cops on the horseback said, line up. And I was like, I'm a little bit of a knife. I was like, I'm a little bit of a knife. I had a knife. I didn't have to cut no bottom of that knife. I just happened to have my pocket. And so I walked down, I was walking from Franklin Street to Gondonely. And over after Gondonely, we went, came towards Lizzie Field. So when I was on the track, I remember I had, crossing the tracks, I remember I had this knife. So I took the knife out of my pocket and dropped it on the track, you know. And so the caddies down on the fifth precinct. So the guy, I went, I asked the guy, the doorman, he knew me because he lived in the next block from me. So he said, what are you doing? I said, well, I don't know. I started a hard work. So I said, what do you tell him about? You know, my father, my mother, when you get off that, I'm here. She said, yeah, well. So I checked my drums. I checked all the guys at home and they put us right in the Black Mariah. They had two horses at that time, you know. They can't see nothing in the Black Mariah, you know. They put you in there and lock you in there. And they took us up to the nightcoats. So I get the nightcoats and all sitting there. I said, I'm guilty, not guilty of me. I said, I'm guilty of you. I told him, he said, you find everybody, two and a half or 30 days or so. And I said, well, I did have $2.25 in my pocket. I remember that very well. I remember that. So I put this in the cell. So one guy said, loan me a quarter because I think he had $2 a quarter. I don't know how it was, but he said, if you loan me a quarter, I'll get out of here. And I go tell you, your daddy or your mommy that you're in jail. And I said, all right. So I gave him a quarter. Everybody seemed like they all got out with me. So one morning, about 7 o'clock, my father came and he paid my fine. And I came on out. That was for nothing. And the next time I went to the Fifth Free Center, I was working at the St. Charles Hotel. I was running the freight elevator. And I was standing on a reported corner, a corner of a reporter. We used to take drumsticks and beat on them and lay the step at that particular corner, two on Murray Street. And we used to whistle and play the sticks. We used to play the sticks. We used to play the sticks. And the other boy I called Scala Brown, he had sticks. And he was pretty good and I was pretty good. And we all could whistle pretty good. Good whistlers. We would whistle ratty, ratty tunes, you know. So this particular afternoon, I didn't stop there very long. I was talking to some guy. And I was on my way to the library theater. And I had my, my fed at the theater, I think it was 10 cents. And I had a nickel for my Johnny Crook. And I was playing what? Johnny Crook, that's a can there. A flat piece of can there, you know. And two cops came up there. One of them, the name of the cops, I can recall that pretty good, was Jesse Youngblood. It was one of the cops. And I remember it was Peru. Peru. So when I seen nothing coming, so I knew to call him the reporter like I'm on. Miss Mary Overhauls, you ought to see. And I wasn't hit behind the door. So they came in and looking around. I was bound to hit behind the door. It looks like the door was open when I was in the corner. And when they came, he came and looked and said, is anybody coming here, Miss? I'll lay down. So she said, no I didn't. I said, yeah I am. So I said, yeah I am. I got scared.
You know, I don't know. What happened? So they took me.
And the other guy took the other guy's horse and was leading the other horse. And the other guy had me heist up like that. Passed right by my mama's house, you know what I mean?
And I said, okay, what are you doing?

I'm going to jail. And a guy had me heist up like that. It's like I had to kill somebody, murder somebody, you know what I mean? So my father, well he's driving, you know, carousel. And he was working on Legendfield, which we began. And they struck from, you know what it was, Dauphine and Legendfield, where Christian Music Club. I got it wrong. I got it wrong. Yeah, I can recall her. And my dad was working for Missy the Undertaker's name again. I'm not sure. Oh, it was a popular name. But anyway, well past then my daddy's here. So he told me he was born and stuff. They got my son born in the precinct. So I went and over all of them in the lab. So he came out and told me to go to the night court. I had to go to the night court. They released me, by the way. They had to go to the night court. So I went to the night court and the judge released me. But that's not the first time I had no, actually when I was a man I went to jail. But when I was a kid I went too, you know. Yeah, I played on the lady's step next door to my house, you know. Oh, you know about that. I don't have to tell you about that. You got that one now. No, I never did that for.
Oh yeah, you got that one now. I gave you that one.

Not cool. Yeah, I was playing on this lady's step. And she said I used to know her, you see. So she had me arrested, see. So when I go to the judge, I could play the sticks pretty good, you know. So the judge said, well, can you play? I said, yeah, that's a good play so I played the job. And he said, well, this judge, man, he gave me 50 cents until I'm going home and don't do that no more. He said, don't play on that lady's step no more. I don't really tell you that one. How old were you? Oh, I was coming up, I was about, oh, I guess I was about 18, 12 or 18, somewhere around there. I can't recall anymore. I didn't keep them with all that, you know. And all that. Wow. Now you said, we're speaking about the dance halls, huh? Yeah, I was wondering, you know, what I mean? Well, about the funerals, you used to ask me about the, you asked me about the funerals? Well, at that particular time, I mean, those years, let's see, there had so many societies that used to turn out with music, you know, and everybody wanted to be buried by music, you know. So they joined these societies, you see, like the Young Men of our Day, the Old Men of our Day, the Liberty, and all so many, I can't recall all those. And even clubs, I mean, would give you music, like the Boots Club, the Lions Club, I mean, they gave you Masonics and all that, they'd have music. And sometimes, guys would belong to maybe three or four organizations that had, that would have music, you see. And, well, the widow would say, well, she wants music, and he wants music, that's what he wants, so he'd get the music. And they'd have, sometimes, three or four bands. Five of them went down and they had four bands.
Four bands.

And I can remember, two good bands, I mean, they had, that was Excelsior and the O.B.B.'s, the Armaid Brass Band. The O.B.B.'s was the best band, in my estimation. Not that my dad played with them, played with that band, but they actually had the best brass band. It was a radded brass band. It was more radded than, they played more radded music than Excelsior. Excelsior played a lot of marches, you know. All of them were good musicians. They were all good leaders. Yeah, that's it. But, I don't know, that would happen most any day they would bury somebody, you know.
Would it be Tuesday, Sunday, Saturday?
No, just any day, but most likely a guy would like to be held over on a Sunday, because everybody would be out to see a procession, you know, go by and see.
But they still did that until, that's quite recently, you know.
Yeah, recently, yeah, yeah. A few years back, I mean, they stopped that.
Well, Sunday's, the Undertaker's won't work on Sunday now, you know.

No, no, no. And then, the Undertaker don't care about your having in the music, because it takes too much time, you see, because the way people die so fast today is that they have time to make two or three funerals in one day, you see. Like, they have a body, they're taking about 8, burry, 8.30 in the morning, well, they have another 10.30, well, by that time, I mean, they're back, you see, they buried that person in that some other other person's house, you know, either back to the Undertaker, whatever, whatever he's laid off there, you know. And that would have a chance to bury, you know, two, three people. So, having music, it takes two more to play those marches, you know, a few more marches, you know.

I wondered if there was anything specially good on, say, Tuesday. How's that? Is Tuesday a good day for any kind of job, a Wednesday, a Thursday? No, not that I can recall, no, no. They wouldn't have dances on a Wednesday march, or?

No, not for the week, no, I mean, lawn parties, like they'd have lawn parties, well, that would always be on Sunday night. And, well, fish fries, you know, fish fries would always be on Saturday night, you see, you'd see the red lantern in there by the gate, you know, where you know that there was fine fishing. Back there, you'd go back in the alley and to the kitchen always lead you to the kitchen, you know, alley leads you to the kitchen. And everybody back there, sitting out eating fish, drinking the old wine, having a good time, you know. Those were really some good days.
What kind of band would they have in a fish?

None of them have no band. I mean, maybe a guy would have a show, have a guitar, they'd be singing or something like that. Oh, everybody would start singing and clapping and doing a number or something like that, be happy, you know. With no music?
No instruments. No instruments.
They just clap and sing. No music. No, people don't clap.
Now any special holidays where they had music?
Special holidays?
Uh huh.

Well, right now for example, we're coming into Christmas. Would they have Christmas parties or any? No, not the lock in the car, no. I mean the people was thinking about the presents of those days and most likely they'll take your dinner, you know. They're thinking about their dinner, you know. They're thinking about the, much about dancing. I can remember. No. While they're skipping their wine together, they're drinking wine for the gumbo, you know, and the turkey dinner. It's traditional, traditional. Still happens, you know, still.
What about New Year's Eve?
New Year's Eve? Well, I mean it's more so now, I can recall, they have more affairs on New Year's Eve. I can recall right now, I mean, at this age, I mean. Yeah, at this age. That's all right.
Any other holidays where they have a music?

Well, a lot of, you know, everybody could come out on a lot of my day. I mean, everybody prepared, you know. Ratch, you know. They had bands of all types of bands, all the way they have. I mean. And masks, because everybody masks in those days. I mean, people had fun. I mean, it's no fun. No fun at all. Everybody looking to push you or something out there where they'll start arguing or fight or something. I don't know those people. They just don't like like no more. You see, those days people liked all the girls. I mean, everybody in the neighborhood, all their friends would get together, maybe 20, 25 of them. And they'd say, well, we're all gonna mask together, see. And they'd wear maybe those baby doll dresses, you know. And bonnets and the YA masks, you know. And it really looks sharp, you know. And they'd have the baby dolls that have different bunches, you know. And they'd get on calling, there'd come somebody with a guitar and maybe a kazoo and a bass drum beating. And you'd see a whole bunch of money, just dancing and shaking in the street. I'm having a good time, man. I'm having fun. You don't see that anymore. What about it? I mean, everybody was masks. You know what I'm talking about? You'd see a guy maybe with a big book in his hand. And he'd get to the corner and put on a book and he'd start preaching about so-and-so-and-so. And if they had a crowd of Creole people around, he'd start preaching in Creole, you know what I mean? And talking about some guy in the crowd, you know. There's somebody's friends or something like that. You know, it was kicks, you know. But that don't happen anymore. Nothing like that happens. I don't know why, I mean, the people on the last year would. No, there's no fun, you know.
Who would be the guys with the kazoo's and guitars?

Oh, well, just anybody with a... Anybody could have to play just a half-one. It could be you or something. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, just take an old guitar and maybe they wouldn't play the guitar, maybe they was choking the strings, you know, on the strings and the singing, you know. But they was having a good time. Black face, you know, had a black face. They had a big old wig on the head, a big hat or something like that. Raggy, you know, raggy clothes, all strings, you know. They had different types of monogues and all sorts of monogues. It was really good in those days. I mean, nothing happens like that. It was incredible.
What's a wire mask like? How would they do that?

Wire mask? Well, a wire mask was like a screen wire, you know. It was made of face, it was painted, but you couldn't see nobody with that mask. Well now? Just like the mask they had today, but it was made of wire. It was like you're taking a paper mask, you know, paper mask, a piece board mask. It fit all around your face, all the same thing.
When you first started playing, did they play different from what they play now on Bourbon Street?
Yes, it was, yeah, definitely. Definitely.
What would be the difference?
Well, just ain't jazz. It ain't that.
What do they play like on Bourbon Street now? Well, it's more commercial, I mean. More commercial. Play slower? Softer?

Oh, in those days I mean I never played no wild music, no fast music, no tempos. I mean there was no Rayshaws tempo, no Tiger Rag tempo. You play Thai Pariah, you play that fast. A few other tunes I mean we play up in tempo. But there's always a beat in tempo. People never wanted to dance to nothing faster than me. Everything was a good full, full beat to me.
Well, you know that article you had, you told to John Norris for Kodam and everything? Yeah. You had quite a bit to say about Bourbon Street that you printed out, you know.
Well, I can't recall.
You said the truth about it, you know, about how there's no feeling in it and all that.
And nothing happens. I mean, it's a job, that's all. It's a job, you can't enjoy yourself. I mean, you want to be playing fast music all night with a lot of noise, I mean no soul.
Well they sort of squeezed you out of Bourbon Street too. Huh? You've sort of been squeezed out of Bourbon Street now.
I imagine so. I'm still going to live I imagine. I mean it. It's a living because you're free somewhere from a place else you know.
Yeah, well that's another thing.

Well, it's facts. I mean, you know, it's facts what I say about Bourbon Street. I mean, any musician, in fact, they got a job, it's a job. I mean, they want to work. I mean, nobody want to make a lot of living. But I mean, the guys should let the people enjoy the music. When the people come to the place, I mean, instead of making all that noise and things, people are sitting there when they want to hear you play something. That they can rock in their seat. I mean, give them a beat that they can rock and enjoy themselves. But why don't you be blasting the ears out of me? I mean, gee, man, wow. I'm very sorry. Who's offended about it? I mean.
Well, that's a fact. I think the musicians agree. Well, facts is facts. I mean, that's all I'm sure. Yeah, well, 174, it's all the guys.
Maybe the guys, maybe the proprietors on Bourbon Street, say, well, who is he to be saying something like that? But it's the facts, you know?
It's all these guys from 174. I blame it on them. I blame it on the guys from 174. Oh.

He wants to know how to, don't forget to mess around and go. But I told him, no I'm going to tell him. I haven't even got a recording on it. He's in the shame. Dickie, I don't know if you run into a good record of Armstrong. Don't forget to mess around. Save it from me, will you please?
I thought you already had one.
I don't have it, no. I don't have it. I was trying to get a reissue. Some guy reissued it.
Yeah, he did.
On some yellow label or something like that. Was it United label?
No, it wasn't United. H-J-C-A. Huh? H-J-C-A.
I know Joe Glazer got after the guys and they ducked on the table with us. You never hear no more of that particular record. But I really wanted to get a record.
We were talking about the difference in music now and in the old days.
Yeah.
Say, now if you play a picnic today or a party or someplace off Bourbon Street, do you play like you did in the old days more or less or more like they do on Bourbon Street?

Well, let's take like for an instance last night. Well, we played a good beat all the way through. We didn't play nothing fast. We played a party last night on 4th Street for double tone party. Everybody enjoyed this stuff. We had a beat. I mean, it was a really great beat. No kidding. That reminds me of the old days. I mean, last night really reminds me of the old days. Had a pretty good band too. We didn't have no piano. We didn't use no piano last night. We had bass, banjo. Like the old time, you know? Like the old days, you know? We had no piano. And you had trouble? I had a trombone, trumpet and clarinet.
You have trouble finding a banjo now?
No, no, I don't have trouble finding a banjo. No. That's a few around. I mean.
